sentences.text: Osteodontornis is an extinct genus of seabirds that contains only one named species, Osteodontornis orri.
This giant bird had a wingspan of 5.5 to 6 meters and stood 1.2 meters tall on the ground.
Its beak comprised about three-quarters of the head length and featured hollow or cancellous bone-filled tooth-like serrations.
A premaxilla tip from Venezuela suggests that the animal could have had a wingspan exceeding 7 meters.
Due to its heavy beak, O. orri likely held its bill between its shoulders during flight, similar to modern pelicans.
O. orri likely nested on high plateaus to facilitate takeoff by walking into the wind.
The genus Osteodontornis was described by Howard in 1957.
The type specimen of Osteodontornis orri was found in Late Miocene shale in California and includes bone pieces and feather impressions.
Fossils of Osteodontornis have been found on both sides of the North Pacific.
O. orri was a seabird that primarily fed on squid and other soft-bodied prey.
The downward-pointing beak serrations were adapted for grabbing slippery pelagic animals like cephalopods, likely snatched from the water during flight or swimming.
Despite its light build, O. orri was likely unable to dive effectively.
Osteodontornis fossils are generally from the Miocene and are often fragmented because the bird had thin and tender bones.
Osteodontornis belongs to the parent group Pelagornithidae and is classified in the family Pelagornithidae.
The genus Osteodontornis is classified in the order Odontopterygiformes, with uncertain close relatives including pelicans, storks, or waterfowl.
Fossils of Osteodontornis date to the Miocene epoch.
Osteodontornis lived from the Thanetian to the Messinian, between 59.24 and 5.333 million years ago.
It is debated whether Osteodontornis is a junior synonym of the genus Cyphornis.

Fossils from Venezuela and Peru might belong to a distinct genus rather than Osteodontornis, and their connection to Atlantic Pelagornis cannot be ruled out because the Isthmus of Panama had not formed yet.
Recent authors divide Neogene pseudotooth birds by geography (Atlantic to Pelagornis, North Pacific to Osteodontornis), but this division remains a hypothesis pending more well-preserved material.
